These changes have been enough to more than offset the increasing expenditures, causing the mill levy to fall from 44.15 mills in 1972 to 20.34 mills in 1976. It appears that the increasing expenditures necessitated by growth within the county have been accompanied by even larger increases in revenue, lessening the tax burden for county residents.
In the two incorporated areas, Hardin and Lodge Grass, the tax burden situation is in striking contrast to the fiscal situation of the county. Hardin shows a large increase in per capita expenditures, a substantial reduction in the proportion of expenditures financed by property taxes and a modest increase in per capita taxable value. The result is that the mun cipal levy in Hardin has risen from 49.66 mills in 1972 to 67.50 mills in 1976 as shown in Table III-8. The situation in Lodge Grass has been similar; taxable value and expenditures have increased, causing the present mill levy to rise to the constitutional limit of 65.00 mills.
The tax burden situations in the four elementary and three high school districts of the impact area are difficult to generalize. Fluctuations in mill levies are associated with state policy as well as with local variations in enrollment and taxable value. Because of the complexity of these relationships, and because only the Hardin school districts are expected to be significantly affected by Westmoreland coal development, little will be said about the other districts.
